## 1 Kings 12: Notes

**v. 1**
- Shechem was a natural place for the meeting. It was central to the land and in powerful Ephraim, so the northerners felt they could speak freely about their complaints there. Rehoboam didn't call them; he went where they had already gathered. (Wesley) https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/1-kings-12.html
- MacLaren calls the choice of Shechem "suspicious." Picking it showed discontent with how dominant Jerusalem had become. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/12-1.htm
- Guzik: Rehoboam was in a weak position, having to meet the ten tribes on their ground. Wesley and Guzik both say that out of 1,000 wives and concubines Solomon had only one known son, and he was a fool. Their lesson: sin is a poor way to build a family. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-12/ ; https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/1-kings-12.html
- Constable isn't sure who chose Shechem. He notes it was a fitting site because of its history of covenant ceremonies (Gen 12; Josh 24). Precept Austin thinks Rehoboam probably chose it to calm the northern tribes. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/12-4.html ; https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-kings-12-commentary

**vv. 2–3**
- Wesley: when the people sent news of Solomon's death, they also called Jeroboam back. Having a man of his standing present would put more pressure on Rehoboam to grant relief. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/1-kings-12.html
- Gill cites Kimchi's reading that the people "had sent" for him, which is why he came back from Egypt. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_kings/12.htm
- Precept Austin: Jeroboam knew he would soon be king because of Ahijah's prophecy (11:26–31). https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-kings-12-commentary

**v. 4**
- The "yoke" stands for oppression: labour on Solomon's building projects, military service and taxes. (Precept Austin) https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-kings-12-commentary
- Wesley: the burden was heavy taxes for the temple, the buildings, the court and the many wives. Since Solomon had abandoned God so badly, it's no surprise he oppressed the people. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/1-kings-12.html
- Guzik and Matthew Henry both point out that the tribes asked nothing about Solomon's idolatry, only about money and labour. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-12/ ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/12-15.htm

**vv. 6–7**
- Guzik: Rehoboam was wise to ask the elders. Their advice reflected that he was not Solomon and had to earn loyalty as himself. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-12/
- Coffman: Rehoboam's father was one of the wisest men in history, but wisdom doesn't pass down by birth. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/1-kings-12.html
- The Biblical Illustrator applies this to "selfish autocracy," the old idea that being great means being served rather than serving. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tbi/1-kings-12.html

**vv. 8–9**
- Guzik points out that Rehoboam turned down the elders before he ever consulted the young men. He picked advisers who already agreed with him ("advice shopping"), so the consultation was just for show. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-12/

**vv. 10–11**
- "Little finger… thicker than my father's waist" means: my power is greater than my father's, and so will my oppression be. Precept Austin calls it foolish and arrogant. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-kings-12-commentary
- Preacher's Homiletical Commentary: boasting doesn't prove courage, and the louder the boast, the weaker the resolve. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/1-kings-12.html

**vv. 12–14**
- Coffman: "scorpions" may mean a cruel spiked lash, or leather lashes with metal or stones set in them. He says the arrogant reply needs no comment. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/1-kings-12.html
- Dilday, quoted by Guzik and Precept Austin: a dozen rash words opened the door to four hundred years of strife and, in the end, the nation's destruction. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-12/
- BibleHub's chapter notes say Rehoboam confused bullying with strength, and cite Proverbs 15:1. https://biblehub.com/1_kings/12.htm

**v. 15: "this turn of events was from the LORD"** (the traditions really differ here)
- **Baptist (Spurgeon):** God is at work even in events caused by men's sin and stupidity. He had no part in the sin, but in a mysterious way he was in it all. Spurgeon compares this to the crucifixion and holds both human free agency and God's rule. https://ccel.org/ccel/spurgeon/sermons42/sermons42.xxxi.html
- **Pentecostal / Calvary Chapel (Guzik):** God guided events but did not *make* Rehoboam sin. He simply let him make the mistakes his heart wanted. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-12/
- **Puritan/Reformed (Poole, Henry):** God "gave up" Rehoboam to his mistake, turned the people against him, and arranged the circumstances. Henry adds that God "hid from his eyes" what would have brought peace. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/12-15.htm ; https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Ki/1Ki_012.cfm
- **Methodist:** the two leading Methodist commentators disagree.
  - Wesley's Notes repeat Poole's wording that God gave up Rehoboam. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/1-kings-12.html
  - Adam Clarke pushes back. The cause was Rehoboam's folly and tyranny, and the text doesn't teach that this "bad doctrine" came from God. The Hebrew *sibbah* means the *revolution* (the turning away) was from the Lord. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/12-15.html
- **Barnes:** human pride and anger carried out God's plans, without overriding human free will. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/12-15.htm
- **Biblical Illustrator:** God's decrees never excuse us from obeying, and Rehoboam could have avoided the blame. One writer it quotes also draws a "divine right" to revolt against relentless tyranny. https://studylight.org/commentaries/tbi/1-kings-12.html

**v. 16**
- "To your tents, O Israel!" was an old battle cry and here a call to rebellion. "Tents" means their homes: they no longer accepted Rehoboam as king. (Precept Austin) https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-kings-12-commentary
- Guzik: they rejected not just Rehoboam but David's whole dynasty. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-12/

**v. 17**
- Coffman: this verse sets up the lasting split into "Israel" in the north and Judah in the south. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/1-kings-12.html

**v. 18**
- Adoram is the same man as Adoniram, who ran forced labour under David and Solomon. (Precept Austin) https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-kings-12-commentary
- Guzik: he was the wrong man to send, famous for harsh forced labour. Sending him was likely Rehoboam's attempt to carry out his threat. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-12/
- Gill: Rehoboam fled, afraid of the same fate. Gill dismisses a supposed gravestone of Adoniram found in Spain as not genuine. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_kings/12.htm

**vv. 19–20**
- Knapp, quoted by Guzik: Rehoboam should have been thankful God's love for David left him even two tribes. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-12/
- Benjamin stayed with Judah because the two were so closely tied. Why God chose Jeroboam remains "somewhat mysterious." (Precept Austin) https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-kings-12-commentary

**vv. 21–24**
- Spurgeon's sermon "This Thing Is from Me" on v. 24 says the split was from God in two ways: as fulfilled prophecy (Ahijah's torn garment) and as punishment. When events are clearly from God they shouldn't be fought, and fighting the larger northern tribes might have ruined Judah. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/spurgeon_charles/sermons/2476.cfm ; https://biblehub.com/sermons/auth/spurgeon/this_thing_is_from_me.htm
- Henry: Rehoboam and the people listened, broke up the army, and accepted the outcome. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/12-24.html
- Precept Austin:
  - Shemaiah is "forth-telling" (speaking God's word now) rather than foretelling.
  - Who "the rest of the people" are is unclear.
  - Rehoboam deserves credit for heeding a true prophet when many kings didn't.

  https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-kings-12-commentary

**v. 25**
- Jeroboam ruled from Shechem and later from Tirzah. (GotQuestions) https://www.gotquestions.org/Rehoboam-and-Jeroboam.html

**vv. 26–27**
- Pulpit Commentary: Jeroboam saw that the three yearly pilgrimage feasts in Jerusalem would revive religious feeling and sweep his dynasty away. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-kings-12.html
- Guzik:
  - Dividing the kingdom didn't release the north from its covenant duties.
  - Jeroboam ignored God's promise to him through Ahijah.

  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-12/
- Precept Austin: God had offered Jeroboam a lasting dynasty (11:38), and he threw it away. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-kings-12-commentary
- BibleHub: his fear is like Saul's (1 Sam 13), with fear of man replacing fear of God. https://biblehub.com/1_kings/12.htm

**v. 28: were the calves meant as images of the LORD?** (commentators disagree)
- **Yes, as images of the true God, but still sin:**
  - Matthew Henry: the calves were meant to stand for the true God of Israel, not Moloch or Chemosh. The idea came from Egypt's bull-god Apis. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhm/1-kings-12.html
  - Guzik thinks this "likely." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-12/
  - Another writer on BibleHub's 12:28 page says no sane Israelite would think a calf was the God of the Exodus, so they must have been images used to worship God. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/12-28.htm
- **No, they were plainly false gods:** Coffman says the plural "gods" rules out the idea that Aaron or Jeroboam was thinking of the LORD. He rejects the modern scholarly view that Jeroboam wasn't turning Israel to idolatry. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/12-28.html
- Guzik: people usually take the easy way, and a local idol beat the long trip to Jerusalem. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-12/
- **Catholic:**
  - The Catholic Encyclopedia says "calf" probably means a young bull, likely life-size. The calves were probably meant as symbols of Yahweh to attract devout Israelites. https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/06628b.htm
  - It also says Jeroboam added a religious schism to the political one. https://studylight.org/encyclopedias/eng/tce/j/jeroboam.html
- **Reformed (Calvin):** Calvin says Jeroboam "corrupted religion entirely." He uses Jeroboam's Israel as a parallel to the Roman Catholic churches of his day: a church in name that had turned to superstition. https://ccel.org/ccel/calvin/institutes/institutes.vi.iii.html
- **Modern scholarship:**
  - Bible Odyssey says the story is told to echo Exodus 32 and paint Jeroboam badly.
  - Many scholars still think his worship was traditional and even directed to Yahweh. On this view the calves were pedestals for the invisible God, like Judah's cherubim.
  - The account may tell us more about later religious struggles than about what actually happened.

  https://www.bibleodyssey.org/articles/the-sanctuaries-at-dan-and-bethel/

**v. 29**
- Bethel lay on the main road into Judah, and Jacob had met God there twice. Dan already had an idol shrine served by Moses' grandson Jonathan (Judges 18). (Constable) https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/12-26.html
- BibleHub: putting shrines at the southern and northern edges cut the tie to Judah and laid claim to the whole territory. It mentions excavations at Tel Dan. https://biblehub.com/q/Why_did_Jeroboam_set_up_golden_calves.htm

**v. 30**
- Guzik: it was a sin when Jeroboam proposed it and a greater sin when the people followed. He sees the world still embracing "a religion created according to taste." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-12/
- Kelly: Dan was the more popular shrine because it was farthest from Jerusalem. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/12-31.html
- GotQuestions: the "sin of Jeroboam" was idolatry, and it replaced God's whole system of worship with a man-made one. https://www.gotquestions.org/sin-of-Jeroboam.html

**v. 31**
- Appointing priests who weren't Levites broke the Mosaic law, along with Deuteronomy 12's command to worship at one chosen place. (BibleHub) https://biblehub.com/q/Why_did_Jeroboam_set_up_golden_calves.htm
- One writer quoted on StudyLight suggests Jeroboam was driven by strong hostility toward the Levites. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/12-31.html

**vv. 32–33**
- Barnes: "He offered upon the altar" shows Jeroboam acted as priest himself, at Bethel. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/12-32.html
- Gill: he did it himself (compare 13:4), which shows the calves were made to be worshipped, at least as images of God. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/12-32.html
- A writer on BibleHub's 12:28 page: the stated reason for the eighth month may have been the later northern harvest, but the real aim was to erase old ties to Jerusalem. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/12-28.htm
- Precept Austin applies Matthew 15:9, worship built on human rules, to this copied feast. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-kings-12-commentary
- Bible Odyssey: scholars see vv. 32–33 as later additions that strengthen the condemnation. https://www.bibleodyssey.org/articles/the-sanctuaries-at-dan-and-bethel/
